name: Fatima Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm campaign lead at Brightwell, which makes household cleaning products, sprays, dishwasher tablets, that sort of thing. My week is mostly planning promotions with the supermarkets, writing the on-pack offers and the TV-style ads we put on social, and checking every claim with the legal team. I've got two people under me. The part I like is making something boring, like limescale, feel a bit funny.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how are things set up?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sam, who's an electrician, self-employed, so his money goes up and down. Brightwell pays below the big household brands, and between rent and Sam's van loan we've only got about three weeks of savings. There aren't many marketing jobs in this town, so I've stayed at Brightwell five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That sounds about right to me, honestly. A lot of noise and not much change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy tool for small jobs and that's it. At work I'd tell the team to use it for first drafts of the offer copy and not worry. With friends I'd say we all got a bit carried away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel safe in the job but not with the money. Sam had a slow August and we nearly missed rent. A plateau doesn't fix that, and Brightwell isn't giving big rises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the chatbot for rough drafts, it saves me maybe an hour a week. I'd try to save a hundred a month in a separate account so Sam's slow months don't scare us. I'd ask for a small rise in spring, three percent or so, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. It's the normal background worry, not a new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened in August, when you nearly missed rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of Sam's big jobs got pushed back and the money came in a month late. We had to put the rent on a credit card. My partner's slow months as an electrician are the thing that keeps me up, not chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever look outside Brightwell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a clear step up. There's a supermarket head office forty minutes away, and they pay more. But I'd want to know it was steady before I moved, because we can't have both of us unsteady at once.

say: I'd call AI a **handy tool** for small jobs, nothing more.
I'd tell my team to use it for **first drafts** and not worry.
think: My job feels **safe**, but money doesn't, after a near miss on rent.
Brightwell isn't giving **big rises**, so the squeeze stays.
do: Use the chatbot for **rough drafts**, saving about an hour a week.
Save **a hundred a month** for my partner's slow months.
Ask for a **three percent** rise in spring.
feel: **Uneasy** but okay, with the usual background worry.
S0.quote: My partner's slow months as an electrician are the thing that keeps me up, not chatbots.
fieldNote: Her worry is **household cash flow**, not technology.
She is **practical** and asks only for modest, safe steps.
She won't move jobs unless it's **steady**, because her partner's income isn't.

steps.text: Keep running supermarket promotions and on-pack offers at Brightwell
Use the chatbot for rough drafts of offer copy
Save a hundred a month in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one feels likely. The checking and planning and writing, that's most of my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to work out what the team's for, now that a lot of drafting is quick. At work I'd volunteer to run a trial so we're ahead of it. With friends I'd say marketing's changing and you either move with it or get moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my two juniors are the ones at risk. Brightwell might not replace them when they leave, and I'd end up managing software instead of people. I think I'd keep my job, but I'm not certain, because the supermarket buyers might start using their own AI to write the promos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a proper course, there's a weekend one the trade body runs for about two hundred and fifty. I'd run the trial at work, starting with legal checks on claims, since that eats so much time. And I'd quietly look at the supermarket head office jobs, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to do, which helps. I'm better when I'm busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd run the trial yourself. Doesn't that speed up the cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But if someone's going to decide how it's used here, I'd rather it was me than a consultant from head office. At least I'd know where the juniors fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sam change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd hold off on the wedding we'd pencilled in for next autumn. A wedding with three weeks of savings and a wobbly job is just a big credit card bill. We'd do a small registry thing instead, maybe.

say: I'd say we need to work out **what the team's for** now.
I'd **volunteer** to run Brightwell's AI trial.
think: My **two juniors** are most at risk of not being replaced.
Supermarket buyers might **write promos** with their own AI.
do: Take the trade body's **weekend course**, about two hundred and fifty.
Run a trial on **legal claim checks** first.
Quietly watch for **head office** jobs nearby.
S1.quote: A wedding with three weeks of savings and a wobbly job is just a big credit card bill.
fieldNote: She prefers to **lead the change** rather than wait for consultants.
Money pressure pushes her to **shrink the wedding**.

steps.text: Take the trade body's weekend AI marketing course
Run an AI trial on legal claim checks at Brightwell
Watch for jobs at the supermarket head office nearby
Swap the planned wedding for a small registry ceremony

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. That's quick. My whole job is thinking work, so that's me in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms and government need to be honest about it fast, and give people some kind of bridge. I'm not one for slogans, but two years is too short to sort anything out. At work I'd say let's be realistic and plan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose my job within a year of it arriving. Sam's work is hands-on, so he gets the three-year gap before robots, maybe more since wiring old houses is fiddly. The thinking parts of his business, the quotes and bookings, would change in 2028 too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start helping Sam on jobs right away, as his mate, to learn the basics. I'd look into an electrical apprenticeship for adults, which takes a few years. We'd live off Sam's money and whatever I could get, and the wedding would be off for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like I'm about to jump off something without seeing the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really retrain as an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. I've watched Sam do it for six years. I'd rather be pulling cable in a cold loft than waiting for a recruiter who's also been replaced by a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, eating out, the gym. Then probably my car, we'd share his van. Sam's van loan has to be paid before anything else, because the van is the business.

say: I'd say firms and government must **be honest** and build a bridge.
I'd say two years is **too short** to sort anything out.
think: I'd lose my job **within a year** of it arriving.
My partner's **hands-on work** gets about three extra years, maybe more.
do: Work as my partner's **electrician's mate** to learn the basics.
Live on his income and **put the wedding off**.
feel: **Alarmed**, like jumping without seeing the bottom.
S2.quote: I'd rather be pulling cable in a cold loft than waiting for a recruiter who's also been replaced by a chatbot.
fieldNote: She immediately sees the **thinking versus hands-on** split in her household.
Her plan is to **join her partner's trade**, not wait.
The **van loan** becomes the one bill that matters.

steps.text: Work as her partner's electrician's mate, then apply for an adult apprenticeship
Live on her partner's income while she trains
Postpone the wedding with her partner
Sell her car and share her partner's van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's tight but you can plan something in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for firms to train their people up, not just cut them. At work I'd ask what Brightwell's plan is. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think marketing has about five years left for me. If I start an apprenticeship now, I'd be qualified around 2030, before the AGI date and well before robots. That's a real plan, which is more than most people would have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrical apprenticeship part-time in the first year, evenings and Saturdays. I'd also take over Sam's quotes and invoices, which saves him time and gets us a bit more work. I'd save hard, maybe a hundred and fifty a month, and keep Brightwell as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a direction. Tired just thinking about the hours, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't Sam's paperwork thinking work that AI will take too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and that's fine, it's only for now. I'd be doing it to help him win jobs while I learn the trade. By 2031 software can do my partner's invoices and I'll be in the loft with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go ahead with the wedding in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but small, maybe in two years when I'm halfway through training. I wouldn't want to wait forever because of a computer.

I'd ask **Brightwell's plan** and keep it practical.
think: Marketing has about **five years** left for me.
Starting now, I'd be **qualified around 2030**, before robots arrive.
do: Start a **part-time apprenticeship** in evenings and Saturdays.

S3.quote: By 2031 software can do my partner's invoices and I'll be in the loft with him.
fieldNote: Five years makes her plan **realistic** rather than desperate.
She treats paperwork help as a **stopgap**, not a career.
She refuses to put life on hold **forever**.

steps.text: Start a part-time electrical apprenticeship in evenings and Saturdays
Take over quotes and invoices for her partner's business
Save about a hundred and fifty a month
Stay at Brightwell as long as they keep her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper amount of time. I could do a lot in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough if we're sensible, no need for panic. At work I'd say let's use the time to get good at the tools and plan the team's future. I'd sound calm, and I think I'd actually be calmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay in marketing for four or five years and use AI more as it gets better. Then I'd move into Sam's business properly, qualified, by the early 2030s. Robots for that kind of work come around 2039, so that's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd keep my job and use the tools more. I'd help Sam with his paperwork on weekends and maybe put money towards a second van so he can take on an apprentice. I'd plan to start my own apprenticeship in year three or four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's the kind of worry you can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is buying a second van a big risk with your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. We'd only do it if Sam had a year of booked work. But a second van means the business can grow while I'm still earning at Brightwell, and that's the time to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next autumn, like we planned. Small, but on time. Ten years is long enough that I'm not cancelling my wedding over a computer.

I'd tell the team to **get good** at the tools and plan ahead.

S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I'm not cancelling my wedding over a computer.
fieldNote: With ten years, her household's **hands-on income** makes her feel safer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be retraining with no savings and no time. What would help is paid apprenticeships for adults, not just school-leavers, so I could earn while I learn. And some help with rent while one of us is training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. Sam and I are one thinking job and one hands-on job. One thinking job and one hands-on job in a household matters a lot, and we're safer than two marketers would be.

headlineQuote: One thinking job and one hands-on job in a household matters a lot, and we're safer than two marketers would be.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old** campaign lead at a cleaning products brand, using AI now and then.
She lives with her partner, a **self-employed electrician**, on about three weeks of savings.
She is **practical**, leads change at work, and worries for her juniors.
In faster pictures she plans to **retrain** as an electrician alongside her partner.
With ten years she feels steadier, and keeps their **wedding** on schedule.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, retraining with no savings and no time.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for adults so she can earn while learning.
**Rent help** while one of them is training.
